question: A 16-year-old male with confirmed JNA (Radkowski stage IIB) is scheduled for surgical resection. What is the essential pre-operative step and its purpose?

answers.text: Pre-operative radiation therapy to shrink the tumour and reduce vascularity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Radiotherapy is not a pre-operative step for JNA. It may be used for recurrent or intracranial extension in selected cases, but surgery remains the primary treatment.

answers.text: Pre-operative selective arterial embolisation 24–48 hours before surgery to reduce intra-operative blood loss

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. JNA receives its blood supply predominantly from the internal maxillary artery (a branch of the external carotid). Selective embolisation of the feeding vessels 24–48 hours before surgery dramatically reduces intra-operative haemorrhage, improving surgical field visibility and reducing transfusion requirements.

answers.text: Pre-operative high-dose corticosteroids to reduce tumour size

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Corticosteroids reduce mucosal oedema but have no meaningful effect on the fibrovascular bulk of JNA. Embolisation is the standard pre-operative preparation.

answers.text: Pre-operative tracheostomy to secure the airway before resection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Routine pre-operative tracheostomy is not required for JNA resection. The essential step is selective arterial embolisation to minimise blood loss.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the management of JNA. The tumour's extreme vascularity means that surgery without prior embolisation carries an unacceptably high risk of intra-operative haemorrhage. Selective arterial embolisation is mandatory preparation.

Well done. Pre-operative embolisation is the cornerstone of JNA management — it converts a potentially haemorrhagic operation into a manageable surgical procedure by devascularising the tumour feeding vessels 24–48 hours before resection.
